title: Accounts from Incomplete Records
outcomes: Explain why records may be incomplete and describe the features and types of single entry (pure, simple, quasi).
Find profit or loss by the capital comparison (statement of affairs / net worth) method and distinguish a statement of affairs from a balance sheet.
Convert incomplete records into double entry using a cash and bank summary, total debtors, total creditors and bills accounts.
Identify hidden drawings and fresh capital, and use the gross profit ratio to estimate missing stock or sales.
Draw up final accounts — trading account, P&L account and balance sheet — when the books are incomplete.

meta.exam_tip: Write the opening statement of affairs, cash summary and total accounts as numbered working notes. Examiners give step marks for each, even when the final balance sheet does not agree.

concepts.title: Why records are incomplete — the "single entry" situation
body: Many small traders and some partnership firms never keep full double-entry books. They usually note cash received and paid, keep personal accounts of customers and suppliers, and rely on the bank statement. Records can also be incomplete because books were destroyed (for example in a fire) or because a key figure such as stock is unknown.

"Single entry" is not a real system: it is simply incomplete double entry — some transactions are recorded in full, some only on one side, and some not at all. The accountant's job is to connect the scraps of information and finish the accounts.

Features: unscientific and unsystematic; real and nominal accounts are generally missing; business and personal cash are mixed; no uniformity between firms; a trial balance cannot be drawn up, so arithmetical accuracy cannot be proved; profit and financial position are only estimates.
concepts.analogy: It is like a diary in which you note who owes you money and how much cash you spent, but never what you bought or sold. You can still guess how the month went — but only roughly.
concepts.work: CAs regularly prepare accounts of small shops, freelancers and family businesses from bank statements, bill files and the owner's notebook — and tax authorities use the same techniques to test whether declared income is believable.

concepts.title: Types of single entry
body: Pure single entry: only personal accounts are kept — nothing about cash, sales or purchases. It exists mostly in theory.
Simple single entry: personal accounts and a cash book. Cash book items are posted only to personal accounts; nothing else is in the ledger.

Quasi single entry: personal accounts, a cash book and some subsidiary books (typically a sales book, purchases book and bills book), plus scattered notes on major expenses like wages and rent. Discounts are usually entered only in personal accounts. This is the most common form used as a substitute for double entry.
concepts.analogy: Pure = only an IOU list; simple = IOU list + cash diary; quasi = IOU list + cash diary + sales and purchase registers.
concepts.work: Before quoting a fee for "writing up the books", a CA first finds out which of these records the client has — it decides whether the conversion method is possible or only the statement of affairs method.

concepts.title: Capital comparison (net worth / statement of affairs) method
body: When only lists of assets and liabilities can be obtained, profit is found by comparing capital at two dates: Profit = Closing capital + Drawings − Fresh capital introduced − Opening capital. A negative answer is a loss.
Drawings are added back because they reduced closing capital without being a business loss; fresh capital is deducted because it raised closing capital without being a business profit.

Capital at each date = assets − liabilities, shown in a Statement of Affairs. Sources: cash book (cash), bank pass book/statement (bank), personal ledger (debtors, creditors), physical count and valuation (stock), and a list of fixed assets at cost less reasonable depreciation.
Remember outstanding expenses (liability), prepaid expenses and accrued income (assets), and depreciation on fixed assets in the closing statement.
concepts.analogy: Weigh yourself on 1 April and again on 31 March; adjust for the extra meals you were given (fresh capital) and the gym sessions you skipped (drawings) — the rest is the real change.
concepts.work: Income-tax officers and banks use the net-worth approach: if a person's wealth grew far more than his declared income plus savings would allow, the gap points to undisclosed income.

concepts.title: Statement of Affairs vs Balance Sheet
body: Both list assets and liabilities, but they are built differently and serve different purposes.

concepts.analogy: A balance sheet is a photograph from the official camera; a statement of affairs is a sketch drawn from memory and a few notes.
concepts.work: When a client's figures are estimates, a CA's report must say so; presenting a statement of affairs as if it were an audited balance sheet would mislead lenders.

concepts.title: Conversion method: completing double entry from the records
body: Better than the net-worth method whenever enough data exist: rebuild the double entry and prepare a proper trading and profit and loss account and balance sheet.

Steps: (1) Find opening capital with an opening statement of affairs. (2) Prepare a cash and bank summary; a missing figure (often cash sales or closing cash) is the balancing figure. (3) Prepare Total Debtors and Total Creditors accounts (and Bills Receivable / Bills Payable accounts) to find credit sales, credit purchases or missing balances as balancing figures. (4) Post the remaining items to nominal and real accounts, make adjustments, and draw up a trial balance and the final accounts.

Total Debtors: Dr — opening balance, credit sales, bills dishonoured; Cr — cash received, discount allowed, sales returns, bad debts, bills received, closing balance. Total Creditors: Dr — cash paid, discount received, purchase returns, bills accepted, closing balance; Cr — opening balance, credit purchases, bills payable dishonoured.

Treatments while converting: private receipts paid into the business (interest on personal investments, legacies, owner's money) are credited to capital; personal payments are drawings; unexplained cash shortages are drawings; expenses shared by home and business (rent of a shop-cum-house) are split on a fair basis such as floor area.
concepts.analogy: You have a jigsaw with a few pieces missing. Each account (cash, debtors, creditors) is a frame; once every other piece is in place, the shape of the hole tells you the missing piece.
concepts.work: Bookkeepers working from bank statements do exactly this every year for small clients: the debtors account reveals sales that never went through the bank, which matters for both GST and income tax.

concepts.title: Spotting drawings and fresh capital
body: Typical hidden drawings: residential share of a common rent, electricity or telephone bill; the owner's life insurance premium paid by the business; household expenses or private loans repaid from business cash; personal gifts; goods or services taken for personal use; collections from customers spent directly on personal needs.

Typical hidden fresh capital: maturity proceeds of the owner's life insurance policy put into the business; interest or dividends on the owner's private investments credited to the business account; rent from non-business property paid in; business creditors paid from the owner's personal money.
Getting these right matters: wrongly treating drawings as expenses understates profit; wrongly treating fresh capital as sales overstates it.
concepts.analogy: Think of two wallets — "shop" and "home". Every rupee that crosses from shop to home is drawings; every rupee crossing from home to shop is fresh capital.
concepts.work: In tax scrutiny, the assessee must explain every large credit in the business bank account; a maturity receipt from an insurance policy is fresh capital, not unexplained income — but it needs documentary proof.

concepts.title: Gross profit technique for missing stock or sales
body: When the business earns a steady gross profit percentage, a memorandum trading account fills in a missing figure: Closing stock = Opening stock + Purchases (+ direct expenses) − Cost of goods sold, where Cost of goods sold = Net sales − Gross profit.
Convert carefully: gross profit of x% on cost = x/(100 + x) of sales. So 25% on cost = 20% of sales; 20% on cost = 1/6 of sales; 33⅓% on cost = 25% of sales.
Use net sales (after returns) and net purchases (after returns); carriage inwards and other direct expenses form part of cost.
concepts.analogy: If every ₹100 of goods you sell earns ₹20, then from total sales you can work back to how much stock must have left the shelves.
concepts.work: The same technique estimates stock lost in a fire or theft and checks whether a client's physical stock figure is plausible.

jobs.title: Preparing a kirana store's accounts for its loan file
jobs.role: Junior accountant at a CA firm
jobs.situation: A grocery owner needs audited-style accounts for a bank loan. He has a sales notebook for credit customers, bank statements, supplier bills and a rough cash diary. No sales total is recorded for cash customers.
steps: List opening assets and liabilities (from last year's return and the owner's confirmation) to find opening capital.
Prepare a cash and bank summary; the shortfall on the receipts side is the probable cash sales.
Build Total Debtors and Total Creditors accounts from the notebook and supplier statements to find credit sales and purchases.
Separate household items paid from the shop (school fees, home electricity) as drawings.
Prepare the trading and profit and loss account and balance sheet; compare the gross profit ratio with similar shops as a reasonableness check.
jobs.takeaway: Every balancing figure is an inference — test it. A gross profit far above the trade average often means some cash expenses or drawings were missed.
jobs.think: The cash summary shows cash sales of ₹14 lakh but the GST returns show ₹9 lakh of cash sales. What do you do?
jobs.answer: Do not simply accept either figure. Look for unrecorded receipts (fresh capital, loans, private income) that were wrongly treated as sales, and discuss the gap with the client — under-reported sales also have tax consequences.

jobs.title: Net-worth test in a tax scrutiny
jobs.role: Tax assistant preparing a reply to a scrutiny notice
jobs.situation: The assessing officer says a trader's net worth rose by ₹9 lakh in two years while declared income was only ₹5 lakh, and proposes to add the difference as undisclosed income.
steps: Rebuild statements of affairs on both dates with the client's documents.
Add realistic household drawings for the period; the officer's estimate may be too high or too low.
Identify fresh capital with proof: gifts from relatives, insurance maturity, sale of an inherited asset.
Recompute the income by capital comparison and compare it with declared income.
jobs.takeaway: The capital comparison method cuts both ways: properly documented fresh capital and realistic drawings can explain an apparent gap.
jobs.think: Why are household expenses added back when testing declared income?
jobs.answer: They were paid out of income, so they reduced the closing net worth. Unless added back, the income earned would be understated.

mcqs.q: Under which type of single entry are personal accounts, a cash book and some subsidiary books maintained?
mcqs.explain: Quasi single entry is the most developed form: besides personal accounts and a cash book, the trader keeps some subsidiary books such as sales, purchases and bills books. Simple single entry keeps only personal accounts and a cash book; pure single entry keeps personal accounts alone. The trap is 'simple single entry', which lacks the subsidiary books. In practice: many small Indian traders fall in this category — a cash book and party ledgers, often in a basic app, but no full double entry.

mcqs.q: Opening capital ₹2,40,000; closing capital ₹2,95,000; drawings ₹36,000; fresh capital introduced ₹25,000. Profit for the year is:
mcqs.explain: Profit = closing capital + drawings − fresh capital − opening capital = 2,95,000 + 36,000 − 25,000 − 2,40,000 = ₹66,000. Drawings are added back because they reduced capital without being a loss; fresh capital is deducted because it raised capital without being a profit. The trap ₹91,000 forgets to deduct the fresh capital. In practice: tax officers use this net-worth comparison to estimate income when a small trader has no proper books.
mcqs.topic: Capital comparison (net worth / statement of affairs) method

mcqs.q: In a Statement of Affairs, capital is:
options: Taken from the capital account in the ledger
Always equal to the opening capital
mcqs.explain: A Statement of Affairs is prepared from incomplete records, so there is no reliable capital account to copy. Capital is found as the balancing figure — total assets minus total liabilities. The trap is 'taken from the capital account in the ledger'; that is how a Balance Sheet gets its capital, because complete double-entry books exist. In practice: a CA helping a small shopkeeper apply for a bank loan first builds a statement of affairs from his bank statements, stock list and party balances.
mcqs.topic: Statement of Affairs vs Balance Sheet

mcqs.q: Debtors: opening ₹45,000, closing ₹52,000; cash received ₹3,10,000; discount allowed ₹4,000; sales returns ₹6,000; bad debts ₹3,000. Credit sales are:
mcqs.explain: Rebuild the total debtors account. Credit side: cash received 3,10,000 + discount 4,000 + sales returns 6,000 + bad debts 3,000 + closing debtors 52,000 = ₹3,75,000. Debit side has opening debtors 45,000, so credit sales (the balancing figure) = 3,75,000 − 45,000 = ₹3,30,000. The trap ₹3,17,000 counts only cash received, omitting discount, returns and bad debts. In practice: when a client's sales register is incomplete, accountants reconstruct sales from the debtors' movement and bank receipts.
mcqs.topic: Conversion method: completing double entry from the records

mcqs.q: Sales are ₹6,00,000 and gross profit is 20% on cost. Gross profit is:
mcqs.explain: Gross profit of 20% on cost means cost 100, profit 20, sales 120. So profit is 20/120 = 1/6 of sales: 6,00,000 × 1/6 = ₹1,00,000. The trap ₹1,20,000 applies 20% directly to sales, which is the rate on cost, not on selling price. In practice: retailers often quote markup on cost while accountants work with margin on sales, so converting between the two is a daily skill.
mcqs.topic: Gross profit technique for missing stock or sales

mcqs.q: Maturity proceeds of the proprietor's life insurance policy deposited in the business bank account should be treated as:
mcqs.explain: Maturity proceeds of the proprietor's personal life insurance policy are his private money. When deposited in the business account, they are fresh capital introduced and credited to his capital account. The trap is treating them as business income or sales, which would overstate profit. In practice: when reconstructing accounts, a CA asks the owner to explain large unusual bank credits — LIC maturities, gifts or loans — so they are not taxed as business receipts.

mcqs.q: Rent of ₹48,000 is paid for premises, one-third of which is used as the owner's residence. The amount charged to the profit and loss account is:
mcqs.explain: Only the business share of rent is a business expense. The owner lives in one-third, so the business uses two-thirds: 48,000 × 2/3 = ₹32,000 charged to profit and loss. The residential one-third, ₹16,000, is drawings. The trap ₹48,000 charges the owner's housing cost to the business. In practice: shop-cum-residence arrangements are very common in Indian towns, and the income-tax law also allows only the business part of such expenses.
mcqs.topic: Conversion method: completing double entry from the records

mcqs.q: Which statement about books kept on single entry is correct?
options: A trial balance cannot be prepared from them
Nominal accounts are always fully maintained
The system is uniform for all firms
mcqs.explain: Under single entry, only some accounts (mainly cash and personal accounts) are kept, so the two aspects of every transaction are not recorded. Without a complete ledger, a trial balance cannot be prepared. The trap 'profit worked out is exact' is wrong — profit under single entry is only an estimate. In practice: a small trader with only a cash diary cannot produce a trial balance, so a CA reconstructs the accounts before filing his return.
mcqs.topic: Why records are incomplete — the "single entry" situation

mcqs.q: Cash and bank summary: opening balance ₹8,000; collections from debtors ₹1,90,000; payments ₹2,40,000; closing balance ₹12,000. Cash sales (not recorded) must be:
mcqs.explain: In the cash summary, total payments side = payments 2,40,000 + closing balance 12,000 = ₹2,52,000. Known receipts = opening balance 8,000 + collections 1,90,000 = ₹1,98,000. The missing receipt, cash sales, = 2,52,000 − 1,98,000 = ₹54,000. The trap ₹62,000 forgets the opening balance, which was also available to make payments. In practice: retailers who don't record counter sales have them reconstructed this way from the cash and bank movement.
mcqs.topic: Conversion method: completing double entry from the records

mcqs.q: Opening stock ₹40,000; purchases ₹2,60,000; sales ₹3,20,000; gross profit 25% on sales. Closing stock is:
mcqs.explain: Gross profit is 25% on sales, so cost of sales = 3,20,000 × 75% = ₹2,40,000. Closing stock = opening stock 40,000 + purchases 2,60,000 − cost of sales 2,40,000 = ₹60,000. The trap is taking 25% as a markup on cost (cost = 2,56,000, stock 44,000). In practice: after a fire or theft, insurers and accountants use this gross-profit method to estimate the stock that should have been on hand.
mcqs.topic: Gross profit technique for missing stock or sales

mcqs.q: Creditors: opening ₹30,000, closing ₹36,000; cash paid ₹1,80,000; bills payable accepted ₹20,000; discount received ₹2,000. Credit purchases are:
mcqs.explain: Rebuild the total creditors account. Debit side: cash paid 1,80,000 + bills payable accepted 20,000 + discount received 2,000 + closing creditors 36,000 = ₹2,38,000. Less opening creditors 30,000 on the credit side: credit purchases = ₹2,08,000. The trap ₹1,88,000 forgets that accepting bills payable also reduces creditors. In practice: when purchase invoices are missing, accountants rebuild purchases from supplier payments and balance confirmations.
mcqs.topic: Conversion method: completing double entry from the records

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT a drawing?
options: Wages paid to shop staff from business cash
Owner's life insurance premium paid from business cash
Goods taken home by the owner
Residential share of a common electricity bill
mcqs.explain: Wages paid to shop staff are a normal business expense charged to profit and loss. The owner's personal life insurance premium, goods taken home and the residential share of electricity all benefit the owner personally, so they are drawings. The trap is the residential electricity share — it is drawings even though it is paid as part of a business bill. In practice: tax audits of proprietors often find personal expenses booked as business costs, and such items are disallowed.

summary: Single entry = incomplete double entry; no trial balance; profit is an estimate.
Types: pure (personal accounts only), simple (+ cash book), quasi (+ subsidiary books).
Capital comparison: Profit = Closing capital + Drawings − Fresh capital − Opening capital.
Conversion method: opening statement of affairs → cash and bank summary → total debtors/creditors (and bills accounts) → final accounts.
Gross profit technique fills in missing stock or sales; convert "on cost" to "on sales" first.
remember: Statement of affairs: capital is the balancing figure.
Bills accepted go to the debit of creditors; bills received go to the credit of debtors.
Private receipts into the business = capital; private payments = drawings.
x% on cost = x/(100 + x) of sales.
traps: Don't forget cash sales/purchases when totalling sales and purchases.
Don't deduct drawings in the capital comparison — add them back.
Don't leave household bills inside business expenses.

viva.q: What do we mean by single entry system, and what are its main features?
viva.model: Single entry is not really a system; it is incomplete double entry, where some transactions are recorded fully, some only on one side and some not at all. Usually only cash and personal accounts are kept and real and nominal accounts are missing. Business and personal cash get mixed, there is no uniformity, a trial balance cannot be prepared, and the profit worked out is only an estimate.

viva.q: Name and explain the three types of single entry.
viva.model: In pure single entry only personal accounts are kept. In simple single entry personal accounts and a cash book are kept. In quasi single entry personal accounts, a cash book and some subsidiary books like the sales book, purchases book and bills book are kept; this is the form most commonly used.

viva.model: Under the capital comparison or net worth method, we find capital at the beginning and at the end by preparing statements of affairs, where capital is assets minus liabilities. viva.q: Give the main differences between a statement of affairs and a balance sheet.
viva.model: A statement of affairs is prepared from incomplete records and estimates, and capital in it is just a balancing figure; omissions are hard to detect. Its purpose is to find capital at the beginning and end of a period. A balance sheet is prepared from ledger balances under double entry, capital comes from the capital account, omissions are detected because it would not agree, and it shows the financial position.

viva.q: How would you find credit sales when the sales figure is missing?
viva.model: Prepare a total debtors account. On the debit side put the opening balance of debtors and bills dishonoured; on the credit side put cash received, discount allowed, sales returns, bad debts, bills received and the closing balance of debtors. The balancing figure on the debit side is credit sales. Adding cash sales from the cash summary gives total sales.

viva.q: Give examples of hidden drawings and hidden fresh capital in incomplete records.
viva.model: Hidden drawings include the residential share of rent or electricity, the owner's life insurance premium paid by the business, household expenses paid from business cash and goods taken for personal use. Hidden fresh capital includes the maturity amount of the owner's insurance policy, interest or dividend on his private investments, or rent from private property put into the business, and business creditors paid from his personal money.

cases.title: Anand Electricals — reconstructing sales
cases.case: Anand Electricals does not record cash sales. Its cash and bank summary for 2025-26 shows: opening balance ₹5,000; collections from debtors ₹1,24,000; cash sales not recorded. Payments: creditors ₹1,50,000; rent ₹12,000; salaries ₹9,000; drawings ₹18,000; closing balance ₹6,000. Debtors were ₹38,000 at the start and ₹47,000 at the end; discount allowed ₹1,500 and bad debts ₹2,000. The trade earns a uniform gross profit of 25% on cost.

mcqs.q: Cash sales for the year are:
mcqs.explain: Payments side of the cash summary = creditors 1,50,000 + rent 12,000 + salaries 9,000 + drawings 18,000 + closing balance 6,000 = ₹1,95,000. Known receipts = opening balance 5,000 + collections from debtors 1,24,000 = ₹1,29,000. Cash sales = 1,95,000 − 1,29,000 = ₹66,000. The trap ₹71,000 ignores the opening balance. In practice: when a dealer doesn't record counter sales, the accountant reconstructs them from the cash and bank movement.
mcqs.topic: Conversion method: completing double entry from the records

mcqs.explain: Rebuild the debtors account. Credits: collections 1,24,000 + discount 1,500 + bad debts 2,000 + closing debtors 47,000 = ₹1,74,500. Less opening debtors 38,000: credit sales = ₹1,36,500. The trap ₹1,33,000 forgets the discount and bad debts, which also reduce debtors without cash coming in. In practice: an electricals dealer's credit sales can be checked this way against GST returns filed for the year.
mcqs.topic: Conversion method: completing double entry from the records

mcqs.q: Gross profit on total sales is:
mcqs.explain: Total sales = cash 66,000 + credit 1,36,500 = ₹2,02,500. A gross profit of 25% on cost equals 25/125 = 20% of sales: 2,02,500 × 20% = ₹40,500. The trap ₹50,625 applies 25% directly to sales, mixing up markup on cost with margin on sales. In practice: a uniform markup lets an accountant cross-check whether the reconstructed sales and purchases make commercial sense.
mcqs.topic: Gross profit technique for missing stock or sales

mcqs.q: If ₹3,000 of the "drawings" was actually rent for the shop, net profit would:
mcqs.explain: If ₹3,000 of the 'drawings' was really rent for the shop, it is a business expense. Moving it from drawings to rent increases expenses by ₹3,000, so net profit decreases by ₹3,000 (capital is unchanged overall, since drawings fall by the same amount). The trap 'not change' forgets that drawings never pass through profit and loss. In practice: misclassifying payments between drawings and expenses changes taxable profit, so a CA checks every large debit.
